prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The shag rug of a Great Plains buffalo, a flightless bird gone to stone: over its fellow keepsakes, into the archives of air, the whale hauled a harvest of dust. In the ripples of glass sealed over songbird skins, I wavered. What could be said for love? From the Full-Serv to the Self-Serv Island at the Gulf station next door, landlocked waves shivered in a row of corn. The great flukes lifted. A Milky Way scarred the underside more vast than the Midwestern night. Dark cargoes would give themselves up to these shallows that waited to take home the sailor, home to the sea of fossilized coral upon whose shoals just down the road the motels of Coralville lay sprawled. Here would lie a ring scratched by a scrivener with florid hand, In thy breast my heart does rest flung back to shore, here rest two coins face to face, joined by the salt that turned them faceless as they turned to each other.

The text opens by assembling a collection of museum-like relics drawn from natural history, arranging them as though behind glass in a hall of quiet preservation. A buffalo rug lies flattened and stilled; a fossilized flightless bird stands as evidence of a vanished lineage; the delicate, preserved skins of songbirds hint at flight long since silenced. Together, these artifacts evoke a sense of archived time—of life caught, catalogued, and held in suspension, so that the reader moves through the passage as through a specimen room where the past is meticulously kept.

At the center of this arrangement stands the figure of the whale, a single dominating image around which the other elements orbit. The whale is imagined carrying dust and dark cargoes, freighted with residue and shadow as it moves toward shallow waters. Those shallows are rendered not as a place of danger but of arrival: they seem to welcome the sailor home, converting the whale's slow approach into a homecoming, a return charged with symbolic weight.

Throughout, the imagery deliberately blurs the boundary between land and sea, refusing to let the two remain distinct. The Midwestern cornfields are recast as "landlocked waves," their rows rolling and cresting like an inland ocean, while the scene reaches back through deep time to the ancient fossilized coral lying beneath Coralville. In this way the poem insists that the prairie is itself a kind of sea—one that has merely dried and hardened, its aquatic memory buried but never wholly erased.

The scale then widens dramatically, as cosmic and geological dimensions converge upon the single body of the whale. A "Milky Way" is said to scar its underside, and the image is startling in its reach: the mark suggests a vastness that rivals, even exceeds, the night sky arching overhead. The whale becomes a vessel large enough to contain galaxies, collapsing the distinction between the immense and the intimate, the celestial and the corporeal.

Finally, the passage narrows once more to close on small, deeply human tokens. An inscribed ring and two coins fused together by salt appear as the last images, their surfaces worn faceless by time and the elements. Yet in their erosion they carry enormous emotional weight, embodying love and connection that persist even as their particular details are dissolved. What remains is not the legibility of the inscription but the endurance of the bond itself—a tenderness outlasting the very words meant to record it.

# The Natural History Museum at Coralville

In the glass cases, everything holds still.
The stone bird waits with folded wings,
its feathers turned to sediment and time,
a creature that will never lift again
into the air it once knew how to hold.
Beside it hangs the whale—or what remains,
the long articulated architecture
of a body meant for depths, now suspended
above a plain that hasn't touched the sea
in three hundred million years of drifting.

And here, the songbird skins, drawer after drawer,
each labeled in a careful, faded hand:
the throats that sang now emptied of their singing,
the small bright bodies flattened into stillness,
preserved against forgetting, though we know
that preservation is its own forgetting,
a way of keeping what we cannot keep.

Outside, the cornfields run to the horizon.
The gas stations glow their sodium orange light.
The Coralville motels stand row on row,
their neon buzzing over parking lots—
and none of us who stop here for the night
remember that we're sleeping on a reef,
that underneath the asphalt and the beds
the ancient coral holds its calcified applause,
a whole drowned ocean pressed beneath Iowa,
the fossil record of a warmer world.

How strange, to find the sea so far from water.
How strange, that love should surface here at all,
among these landlocked artifacts of loss.

But love does surface. In the museum shop,
or somewhere in the drawers of memory,
I think about the ring you gave to me,
its inside band engraved with our two names
and a date that meant beginning—how the words
were worn now, almost smooth beneath my thumb,
the way a river smooths the stone it passes.
Such a small thing to carry so much weight.

And I remember reading once about
two coins recovered from a foundered ship,
fused into one by centuries of salt,
the ocean's chemistry that would not let them part—
two separate faces melted into one,
made permanent by the very thing
that should have worn them both to nothing.

This is what I want to understand:
how the smallest human tokens outlast
the vast indifferent turning of the earth.
The whale becomes a fossil. Stars burn out.
The coral that was ocean becomes stone,
becomes a town, becomes a place to sleep.
And still the ring holds fast its two engraved names.
And still the coins refuse to come apart.

Against the geologic dark, against
the cold arithmetic of cosmic time,
we have these little proofs that we were here—
that someone loved, and left a mark to say so,
that intimacy, though it cannot last,
is not therefore made meaningless, but rather
gains its terrible sweetness from its ending,
the way a note is precious for its silence,
the way the songbird's skin still holds the shape
of everything it was, and everything it sang.

So let the museum keep its careful dead.
Let Coralville sleep on above its reef.
I'll hold the ring. I'll think about the coins.
I'll carry these small mercies through the night,
these fragile human things that somehow stay,
that somehow, against all the odds, endure.

# The Great Plains

The Great Plains is a vast expanse of flat land that stretches across the central portion of North America. This immense region spans from the Canadian provinces in the north down through the United States, covering parts of ten states including Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas. Extending eastward from the Rocky Mountains, the Great Plains form one of the most significant geographical features of the continent.

## A Land of Grass and Sky

The defining characteristic of the Great Plains is its seemingly endless grassland. Historically, this region was covered by prairie grasses that supported enormous herds of bison. The landscape appears deceptively simple, but it contains a rich diversity of ecosystems shaped by varying levels of rainfall, temperature, and soil composition. The open terrain and wide horizons have earned the area nicknames like "the sea of grass."

## Historical Significance

The Great Plains hold deep cultural importance, particularly for the many Native American tribes who lived there for thousands of years. Nations such as the Lakota, Cheyenne, Comanche, and Pawnee developed sophisticated cultures centered around the bison and the rhythms of the land. Later, the region became a crucial part of American westward expansion, as pioneers crossed the plains in wagon trains seeking new opportunities.

## Agricultural Heartland

Today, the Great Plains serve as the agricultural backbone of North America. Often called the "breadbasket," this fertile region produces vast quantities of wheat, corn, and other grains. Cattle ranching also remains a vital industry throughout the area. The rich soil and expansive farmland make the Great Plains essential to food production on both a national and global scale.

## Conclusion

The Great Plains represent far more than empty space on a map. This remarkable region embodies natural beauty, historical depth, and economic importance. From its ancient grasslands to its modern farms, the Great Plains continue to play a central role in the story of North America.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about visiting a natural history museum in Iowa, weaving together a whale skeleton, taxidermied birds, buffalo, and the surrounding Midwestern landscape with its cornfields and gas stations.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Prairie Remembers

In Iowa, where the land lies flat as a held breath, I came to a building of stone and entered the memory of the world.

There, suspended in the vaulted air, hung the bones of a whale—each vertebra a small cathedral, each rib a curve of longing. Impossible leviathan, how did you swim so far inland? The sea that once swallowed this continent has receded into deep time, leaving you stranded in fluorescent light, your great skull dreaming of pressure and salt and the black weight of water. Above the cornfields, you float. Below you, children point and gasp, not knowing they too are made of oceans.

The birds do not sing here. They perch in permanent attention, glass-eyed sentinels of a stopped hour—the cardinal frozen mid-flare, the owl caught in its swivel of silent judgment, the passenger pigeon that flies now only in the imagination, extinct as a rumor. Their feathers hold the dust of decades. Someone, long ago, arranged these wings just so, believing that to preserve a thing is to keep it from vanishing. But look how still they are. Look how the stillness aches.

And the buffalo—oh, the buffalo—shoulders like mountains, head bowed as if in grief or prayer. It stands upon a diorama of painted grass, the same grass that once rolled unbroken from horizon to horizon, thundering with hooves, dark rivers of the living moving across an unfenced world. Now it is one, and it is quiet, and behind its molded body a mural pretends at endlessness.

Outside, the real Iowa waits.

The cornfields stretch in their green militias, row upon obedient row, feeding a hunger that never learns its own name. The gas stations glow at the crossroads like small false suns, humming with the smell of diesel and burnt coffee, where travelers pause to fill their tanks and empty their bladders and buy the sugared things that keep them moving. Here is the present tense, relentless, ordinary, holy in its way.

I stood between these worlds—the whale's ancient sea and the highway's endless asphalt, the buffalo's vanished thunder and the corn's engineered abundance—and understood that a museum is only a place where we admit what we have loved and lost, what we have killed to keep, what we cannot bear to let dissolve completely into the forgetting land.

The prairie remembers everything. It holds the shell and the bone, the feather and the fossil, the migrations and the extinctions, patient beneath its blanket of soybeans and interstates.

I drove home at dusk, the sky the color of the inside of a shell, and every mile marker seemed a small vertebra in some larger spine, some skeleton of memory stretching out beneath the cornfields, beneath the gas stations, beneath the flat and holy dark—

the whole state a museum with no walls,

the whole world a thing we are always, tenderly, losing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, imagistic piece of poetic prose that connects a fossilized whale to the ancient sea that once covered the American Great Plains, meditating on love, memory, and objects left behind.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Whale in the Wheat

There is a whale beneath Kansas.

Not the ghost of one, not the idea—but the actual architecture of a body, its vertebrae stacked like a colonnade in the dark, each bone a room where the sea used to live. Sixty million years the wheat has grown above it, oblivious, its roots grazing the ancient ribs like fingers passing over a face they cannot see. The farmer plows and does not know he steers his blade above a cathedral. The combine hums its harvest-song across a graveyard of leviathans.

*

Once, this was the Western Interior Seaway, a warm and shallow water splitting the continent from ice to gulf, and the light came down through it green as bottle-glass. Imagine the whale then—no, not a whale, its ancestor, some long-toothed swimmer, mosasaur or the early cetacean dream of one—moving through that drowned world like a thought moving through a mind. It did not know it swam above the future. It did not know that water is only borrowed, that every sea is a tenant, that the plains were waiting underneath like a held breath.

*

This is what the earth does with what it loves: it keeps it. Not gently. Not as we would keep a letter or a lock of hair, pressed flat in the weight of a book. The earth keeps by *pressure*, by the slow conversion of the tender into the permanent, calcium becoming stone becoming the negative space of stone. What remains is not the animal but the animal's absence, filled. A fossil is a memory the world made of a thing after the thing had gone—the shape of longing rendered in mineral, the exact dimensions of a vanishing.

*

I think of this and think of you.

I think of how we, too, leave the imprint before we leave the room. How love is mostly sediment—the accumulation of small settlings, the coffee cup, the borrowed sweater, the particular silence you kept on the left side of the bed. When you are gone these will not vanish. They will *harden*. They will become the fossil record of a warmth, and someone plowing through the afterward of me will strike them and not know what ocean once moved here, what enormous gentle thing once swam the shallow light of an ordinary Tuesday.

*

The whale did not choose to be remembered. That is the mercy and the horror of it. It simply lived, and sank, and let the patient sediment do its arithmetic. There was no plaque, no wanting to be found. And yet: found. Pulled up into a museum's cool cathedral, wired back into the posture of swimming, so that children press their hands against the glass and feel—what? Something old. Something that says *the world was different and was full.*

*

We are all of us leaving objects in a sea that will dry.

The plains were water. Your hands were mine. Both facts are true and both are past, and both are somehow *still occurring* in the only place they can—in the pressed and darkened strata where the earth keeps what it loved by keeping the shape of what it lost.

Somewhere under the wheat, a whale is still swimming.

Somewhere under the wheat, the sea remembers it was a sea.

And I, above the both of them, walk out into the gold and moving grass and think: *let me leave a good fossil. Let the shape of my loving be the kind they dig up gently, and marvel at, and cannot help but understand.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem set in Coralville, Iowa, that blends museum specimens, fossils, an old inscribed ring, and two corroded coins into a reflection on love and decay.
counterfactuals.output:
# Deaccession

*Coralville, Iowa — where the sea forgot itself*

---

Consider the Devonian: this town named for a reef that no longer knows it is a reef. Four hundred million years of forgetting, and still the limestone keeps its brachiopods like a mouth keeps the shape of a word after the word is gone.

I have been to the museum where they file the dead by kingdom.

*

Here, a drawer of crinoids—sea lilies, they were called, though they were animals pretending at botany, a stem, a calyx, arms that fed on drift. Love does this too. Grows a false root. Insists it is planted when it is only holding on.

*

The ring came from an estate sale off First Avenue, fifty cents in a coffee can. Inside the band, worn nearly to rumor: *forever, or a name that starts with a wound.* I could not read it. The gold had eaten its own promise. Someone meant this. Someone slid it past a knuckle and believed the metal would outlast the hand.

The metal did. The hand did not. This is the only vow that keeps.

*

*Specimen note:* what we call *fossil* is not the creature. It is the absence the creature left, filled slowly with the patience of minerals. The shell dissolves. The mud remembers. You are not loving the person. You are loving the cavity they pressed into you, backfilled now with harder stuff.

Coralville, I am trying to tell you something about erosion.

*

Two coins, corroded past denomination. Green with the long kiss of oxygen. I found them in the same can as the ring and I have decided—because meaning is a thing we salt onto ruin—that they belonged together. Fare for two crossings. Eyes for two closed sets of eyes. Whatever they bought is spent. Whatever they were worth is now only the fact of their staying.

*

Decay is not the opposite of love.
Decay is love shown its own reflection in slower water.

*

The reef did not choose to become a town. The coins did not choose their green. The ring did not choose to keep saying *forever* into an empty finger of air in a drawer in a case in a building where children press their hands against the glass and ask their mothers *was this alive.*

*Yes,* the mothers say. *A long time ago.*

*It still is,* I want to correct them. *Look how it holds its shape. Look what it will not let go of.*

*

I put the ring back in the can.
I keep the coins.
I keep the crinoid's ghost in the limestone under my whole walking life.

In Coralville, the sea is four hundred million years absent
and has not stopped being water where it counts.

---

*This is the exhibit.
This is the wall text.
This is the small brass placard that says:
here is what remained
after the remaining was all
there was left to do.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
# The Cetacean Archive

The whale hangs where no whale should be, a thousand miles from any tide, its bones suspended on wires so fine they seem like threads of thought holding memory aloft. Here, in the belly of the archive, the prairie has forgotten itself and become ocean again—as it was, as it will be, in the long geologic patience of the land.

Look how the ribs curve like the hull of something drowned and resurrected, each vertebra a stepping stone across an absence. The great skull tilts downward, mouth agape, as though it might still filter the dust motes that drift like plankton through the amber archive light. It swims through nothing. It swims through everything. It swims through the accumulated silence of a room where footsteps hush themselves to reverence.

Outside, the corn stands in its regimented rows, oblivious to the ancient sea that pressed this earth flat, that laid down the limestone bed on which the farmers now build their certainties. But the whale remembers. The whale is a rumor of water in a landscape that has traded its ocean for wheat, its depths for the shallow promise of soil.

How strange, this longing that rises when we stand beneath it. Not for the whale alone, but for all the vanished vastness it implies—the pods that sang across distances we cannot fathom, the mothers who nudged their calves toward the surface and the surprise of air. Now only structure remains. Only the architecture of a life, dismantled and reassembled, the marrow long since surrendered to time.

The archivist walks past with her cart of catalogued things, and does not look up. She has grown accustomed to the impossible. But the visitor—the one who pauses, who feels the room tilt into blue—she understands that this is what we do with our grief: we hang it in the light, we label it, we preserve the shape of what we could not keep.

The whale will never touch water again. And yet it swims, endlessly, through the dry sea of our remembering, buoyed by the one element that outlasts all oceans: our terrible, tender need to hold on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a surreal, elegiac prose poem that transforms a small-town Iowa scene—gas station, motels, cornfields—into an oceanic vision haunted by extinct creatures and lost keepsakes.
counterfactuals.output:
# Nocturne for the Landlocked

Here at the edge of Route 9, where the Sinclair sign burns its green apatosaurus against the dark, the pumps stand like buoys marking a harbor that forgot it was ever a harbor. Listen: the corn is not corn tonight. The corn is kelp, ten thousand acres of it, swaying in a current that moves without wind, and somewhere in that swaying the ammonites turn their spiral shells, patient as clocks that gave up telling time.

The motels have names that were always prayers. *Starlite. Dew Drop Inn. The Wagon Wheel.* Their neon flickers underwater now, each vacancy sign a lure dangling in the black, and the salesmen sleeping in Room 6 dream they are drowning gently, dreaming of the mothers who buttoned their coats against a cold that no longer exists.

I have come to look for what the tide took.

My grandmother's thimble. The blue marble I swallowed at seven and was told would surface in a week. The letters my father never sent, their ink dissolving into the general salt. They are all here, drifting through the intersection where the one stoplight sways like an anglerfish, casting its red, its yellow, its green benediction over nothing, over no one, over the great migration of the vanished.

Do you see them? The passenger pigeons, uncountable, schooling now like herring through the Casey's parking lot, their wings the sound of surf. The Carolina parakeets, gold and green as drowned sunlight. And there—dragging itself across the asphalt seafloor—the last of something that has no name because we killed it before we thought to ask.

The gas station attendant is a saint of the abyss. He has been standing at the register for a hundred years, giving directions to travelers who are already ghosts. *Take the county road until the fields become water. You'll know it when your headlights fill with fish.* He does not sleep. He guards the register like a reliquary, and inside it, instead of coins, the small bones of everything we chose to forget.

Outside, the grain silos rise like the vertebrae of a leviathan beached on its back, ribs open to the moon, and the moon itself is a jellyfish, translucent, pulsing, indifferent, trailing its long threads of light down through the flooded rows.

O my town. O my sunken cathedral of the ordinary.

Somewhere a screen door is still opening. Somewhere a mother is still calling a name across the yard, and the name goes out like a lantern lowered into deep water, down and down, past the trilobites clicking in the gravel, past the great extinct silences, until it reaches the child who never came home, who is here, who was always here, curled in the warm dark of the elevator, breathing the amber, waiting for the tide to remember how to rise.

The pumps click off. The tanks are full of ocean.

And the corn keeps swaying, keeps swaying, keeps swaying its green farewell.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
